notes: Slice 'essay': source material for the opening prose 'What Privacy Is: A Short History of an Idea'. Contents: 45 facts (one-sentence statements, each with 1-4 sources carrying verbatim quotes), 16 pull quotes, a 7-paragraph outline (every fact is placed once), 2 quantities and 5 myths. No mapped events - chronology lives in the other slices; facts here overlap with some of them (Warren and Brandeis, BVerfG 1983, UDHR/ICCPR, IEEE 7012, the cypherpunks) by design so the essay can stand alone. METHOD: every CONFIRMED quote was fetched with tools/fetch-text.py and passed --check (all 2026-09-23). Where the canonical host blocks scripts (bepress/Digital Commons repositories, Legifrance, OHCHR, Wiley), the quote was read from an Internet Archive copy (URL given as read) or from another official copy (French Interior Ministry PDF for Code civil art. 9; University of Minnesota Human Rights Library for General Comment 16; Crossref API for the Altman 1977 abstract; Quran.com API for Qur'an translations). Several classic statements are quoted through reliable secondary scholarship because the books are in copyright and not openly online: Westin 1967 (via Solove 2002 and Frontiers in Veterinary Science 2022), Thomson 1975, Gavison 1980, Moore 1984 and Miller 1971 (via Solove 2002), Arendt 1958 (via Komamura 2019, Washington University Law Review), Altman 1977 (publisher abstract plus Acquisti et al. 2020). Each such source note says so. COULD NOT VERIFY / GAPS: OED first-use dates (subscription) - Etymonline and Merriam-Webster disagree on the earliest 'privacy' form (Etymonline: privatie late 14c., privacy 1590s; M-W: 15th century), stated as such; Lewis & Short (Perseus) entry text for privo is not extractable by the helper; the attribution of 'la vie privée doit être murée' to Royer-Collard (1819) or Talleyrand is unverified - Littré gives it unattributed; Rybczynski's Home and Ariès/Duby's History of Private Life were not read directly (architecture facts rest on Solove 2002, which cites them); the Mishnah fact's 'measure of privacy' is a modern translator's gloss; the Constitute count (171/188) is our own computation from its API and reflects text-based coding; Fred Cate's critique of notice-and-choice was not added; Doc Searls's own weblog returns 403 to scripts, so his 2019 Linux Journal column and the ProjectVRM post are used instead. Contested points are flagged contested:true (Chinese yinsi and traditional Chinese privacy; Littré maxim attribution). HOUSEKEEPING: the session scratchpad is shared between researchers; during this run I inadvertently executed another researcher's scratchpad build.py (which had overwritten mine), which rewrote research/verify/dataprotection-2.json from that researcher's own script - the content should be identical to what their script produces, but the owner may wish to re-run it.

facts.statement: The English word 'private' comes from Latin privatus, 'set apart (from what is public), belonging to oneself (not to the state)', the past participle of privare, 'to bereave, deprive, rob, strip' - so the root carries both 'one's own' and 'deprived of'.

sources.institution: Online Etymology Dictionary (Douglas Harper)
sources.title: private (adj.)
sources.quote: from Latin privatus "set apart (from what is public), belonging to oneself (not to the state), peculiar, personal," used in contrast to publicus , communis.
sources.note: Etymonline is a compiled dictionary that draws on the OED, Barnhart and Klein; spacing before commas is as rendered on the page. Lewis & Short (Perseus) gives privo as "To bereave, deprive, rob, strip" but its entry text is not extractable by the repo helper.

sources.institution: Online Etymology Dictionary (Douglas Harper)
sources.title: private (adj.)
sources.quote: This is a past-participle adjective from the verb privare "to bereave, deprive, rob, strip" of anything; "to free, release, deliver" from anything, from privus "one's own, individual,"

facts.statement: The noun 'privacy' is recorded in English from the 1590s (earlier 'privatie', late 14th century), first meaning a private matter or secret, then seclusion; the sense 'freedom from intrusion or interference' is dated to 1814.

sources.institution: Online Etymology Dictionary (Douglas Harper)
sources.title: privacy (n.)
sources.quote: 1590s, "a private or personal matter, a secret;" c. 1600 as "seclusion, state of being in retirement from company or the knowledge and observation of others," from private (adj.) + abstract noun suffix -cy . Meaning "state of freedom from intrusion or interference" is from 1814. Earlier was privatie (late 14c. as "secret, mystery;" c. 1400 as "a secret, secret deed; solitude, privacy"), from Old French privauté .
sources.note: Dictionaries differ on the first date: Merriam-Webster gives the 15th century for its sense 1a, reflecting the Middle English privatie/privetee forms. Treat "late 14th-15th century (as privatie), 1590s (as privacy)" as the safe statement.

facts.note: Merriam-Webster (https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/privacy) shows "15th century, in the meaning defined at sense 1a"; the OED was not consulted (subscription).

facts.statement: Hannah Arendt argued in The Human Condition (1958) that for the ancient Greeks privacy was 'privative' - a life lived only in private was deprived of the public realm and 'not fully human' - whereas modern privacy's 'most relevant function' is 'to shelter the intimate'.

sources.institution: Washington University Law Review (vol. 96, no. 6)
sources.title: Keigo Komamura, 'Privacy's Past: The Ancient Concept and Its Implications for the Current Law of Privacy'
sources.quote: In ancient feeling the privative trait of privacy, indicated in the word itself, was all-important; it meant literally a state of being deprived of something, and even of the highest and most human of man's capacities.
sources.note: Komamura quotes Arendt verbatim (Hannah Arendt, The Human Condition, University of Chicago Press, 1958; p. 38 of the 2nd ed., 1998). The book itself is in copyright and was not read from a publisher copy.

sources.institution: Washington University Law Review (vol. 96, no. 6)
sources.title: Keigo Komamura, 'Privacy's Past: The Ancient Concept and Its Implications for the Current Law of Privacy'
sources.quote: The decisive historical fact is that modern privacy in its most relevant function, to shelter the intimate, was discovered as the opposite not of the political sphere but of the social, to which it is therefore more closely and authentically related.
sources.note: Komamura (pp. 1344-45) quotes Arendt, The Human Condition (1958), p. 38, verbatim. His own abstract adds: "privacy has been a relational concept since the beginnings of western political thought."

facts.statement: Greek thought drew the first map: Aristotle's split between the household (oikos) and the political community (polis) is the usual starting point for philosophical discussions of privacy, and his Politics contrasts what is one's own (idion) with what is common (koinon).

sources.institution: Washington University Law Review (vol. 96, no. 6)
sources.title: Keigo Komamura, 'Privacy's Past: The Ancient Concept and Its Implications for the Current Law of Privacy'
sources.quote: In the ancient Greek thought, political community (polis) is not just different from but stands in direct opposition to the natural community whose center is the home and the family (oikos).
sources.note: Komamura, p. 1341, paraphrasing Arendt, The Human Condition (1998 ed.), p. 28: "the distinction between a private and a public sphere of life corresponds to the household and the political realms".

sources.institution: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Beate Roessler and Judith DeCew)
sources.title: Privacy (substantive revision 19 October 2023)
sources.quote: Aristotle's distinction between the public sphere of politics and political activity, the polis , and the private or domestic sphere of the family, the oikos , is the starting point for philosophical discussions of privacy ( Politics 1253b, 1259b).
sources.note: Spacing around "polis ," and "( Politics" is as extracted from the HTML (italic tags).

sources.institution: MIT Internet Classics Archive (Benjamin Jowett translation)
sources.title: Aristotle, Politics, Book Two, Part III
sources.quote: For that which is common to the greatest number has the least care bestowed upon it. Every one thinks chiefly of his own, hardly at all of the common interest; and only when he is himself concerned as an individual.
sources.note: Politics 2.1261b33-35. Greek (Perseus, Perseus:text:1999.01.0057): "ἥκιστα γὰρ ἐπιμελείας τυγχάνει τὸ πλείστων κοινόν: τῶν γὰρ ἰδίων μάλιστα φροντίζουσιν, τῶν δὲ κοινῶν ἧττον" - koinon (common) against idion (one's own). The Greek was read on Perseus but the repo helper cannot extract it, so the English is quoted.

facts.note: For the Greek idion/koinon vocabulary see the Aristotle fact. Aristotle here argues about property and care, not "privacy" in the modern sense; use it for the vocabulary of own vs common, not as an ancient privacy right.

facts.statement: The Chinese word for privacy, yinsi (隐私), joins yin, 'hide', and si, 'private'; legal scholar Cao Jingchun wrote in 2005 that it has been translated as 'privacy', 'personal secret' or 'shameful secret' and that Chinese people initially often misunderstood privacy as relating to shameful secrets.

sources.institution: Victoria University of Wellington Law Review (vol. 36, no. 3)
sources.title: Cao Jingchun, 'Protecting the Right to Privacy in China'
sources.quote: Yin and si are two words in Chinese: yin means "hide" and si means "private".
sources.note: The PDF text has lost the Chinese characters; Cao distinguishes two near-homophones (commonly written 阴私, a shameful secret, and 隐私, privacy). Characters in the statement are supplied from the NPC source below, not from Cao.

sources.institution: Victoria University of Wellington Law Review (vol. 36, no. 3)
sources.title: Cao Jingchun, 'Protecting the Right to Privacy in China'
sources.quote: It was initially common for Chinese to misunderstand privacy as relating to shameful secrets.

facts.note: Contested: whether traditional China lacked a privacy concept is debated; Cao himself argues privacy "was protected, to some extent, in ancient China" though neither the word nor the modern concept existed.

facts.statement: China's Civil Code (2020), Article 1032, gives the word a legal definition: privacy (隐私) is a natural person's tranquillity of private life and the private space, private activities and private information that they do not wish others to know.

sources.institution: National People's Congress of the People's Republic of China (npc.gov.cn)
sources.title: “典”亮我们的生活丨“个人隐私”不可侵扰 (Civil Code explainer, with text of Arts. 1032-1033)
sources.quote: 隐私是自然人的私人生活安宁和不愿为他人知晓的私密空间、私密活动、私密信息。
sources.note: Translation: "Privacy is a natural person's tranquillity of private life and the private space, private activities and private information that he or she does not wish others to know." The page also states that before the Civil Code Chinese law used the term 隐私权 without defining it.

facts.statement: Japanese uses the loanword puraibashii (プライバシー), a phonetic rendering of the English 'privacy'; Japan's data-protection chairman Masao Horibe has said it spread after the Tokyo District Court recognised a right to privacy for the first time in 1964, in a suit over Yukio Mishima's novel After the Banquet.

sources.institution: Personal Information Protection Commission, Japan (speech by Chairman Masao Horibe, ICDPPC, Hong Kong)
sources.title: Privacy Culture and Data Protection Laws in Japan
sources.quote: In the ruling on the case in 1964, the Tokyo District Court recognized privacy as a right to be protected under the Japanese law for the first time in history.

sources.institution: Personal Information Protection Commission, Japan (speech by Chairman Masao Horibe, ICDPPC, Hong Kong)
sources.title: Privacy Culture and Data Protection Laws in Japan
sources.quote: Due to this court decision and many other backgrounds, the Japanese term of "puraibashii", which is a phonetic spelling of an English word "privacy", has been widely used in our society.

sources.institution: Japan Institute for Labour Policy and Training (JILPT Report No. 14)
sources.title: Ryoko Sakuraba, 'Protection of Personal Information and Privacy in the Japanese Workplace'
sources.quote: Tokyo District Court (28 September 1964), 15-9 Kaminshu 2317.
sources.note: Gives the exact date of the "Utage no Ato" (After the Banquet) judgment. The katakana プライバシー is standard Japanese orthography and is not quoted from these sources.

facts.statement: German has two words for two ideas: the everyday Privatsphäre, a protected 'narrower realm of personal life', and informationelle Selbstbestimmung, the right to 'informational self-determination' that the Federal Constitutional Court recognised on 15 December 1983 - the individual's authority, in principle, to decide on the disclosure and use of their personal data.

sources.institution: Bundesverfassungsgericht (Federal Constitutional Court of Germany), official English translation
sources.title: Judgment of the First Senate of 15 December 1983, 1 BvR 209/83 et al. (Census Act)
sources.quote: This fundamental right confers upon the individual the authority to, in principle, decide themselves on the disclosure and use of their personal data.

sources.institution: Bundesverfassungsgericht (Federal Constitutional Court of Germany), official English translation
sources.title: Judgment of the First Senate of 15 December 1983, 1 BvR 209/83 et al. (Census Act)
sources.quote: Restrictions of this right to 'informational self-determination' are only permissible if they serve an overriding public interest.

sources.institution: Digitales Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (DWDS), Berlin-Brandenburgische Akademie der Wissenschaften
sources.title: Privatsphäre
sources.quote: engerer Bereich der persönlichen Lebensführung, der gegenüber anderen Personen bzw. der Öffentlichkeit besonderen (zum Teil rechtlichen) Schutz genießt
sources.note: Translation: "narrower sphere of personal conduct of life, which enjoys special (in part legal) protection against other persons or the public".

facts.statement: French speaks of vie privée, 'private life', and pictures it walled: Littré's 19th-century dictionary illustrates the term with the maxim 'private life must be walled in', and since the law of 17 July 1970 Article 9 of the Civil Code has given everyone 'the right to respect for his private life' - without defining it.

sources.institution: Ministère de l'Intérieur (France)
sources.title: Article 9 du code civil (loi du 17 juillet 1970)
sources.quote: Chacun a droit au respect de sa vie privée.
sources.note: Translation: "Everyone has the right to respect for his private life." Legifrance (the official code site) blocks scripted access; this is a French government reproduction.

sources.institution: Ministère de l'Intérieur (France)
sources.title: Article 9 du code civil (loi du 17 juillet 1970)
sources.quote: La notion de vie privée n'est pas définie par la loi.
sources.note: Translation: "The notion of private life is not defined by the law." The page adds that case law has filled it in (health, love life, image, religion, family relations, intimacy).

sources.institution: Littré, Dictionnaire de la langue française (online edition, littre.org)
sources.title: privé
sources.quote: La vie privée doit être murée, il n'est pas permis de chercher et de faire connaître ce qui se passe dans la maison d'un particulier.
sources.note: Littré gives the maxim without attribution. It is widely attributed to Pierre-Paul Royer-Collard (c. 1819) and sometimes to Talleyrand (Stendhal, 1823); the attribution was not verified from a primary source.

facts.note: Attribution contested - quote it as Littré's, not Royer-Collard's.

facts.statement: In Arabic-Islamic usage the idea closest to privacy is often hurma - what is sacred or unlawful to look at without permission, including the home - alongside awrah, what must be covered; the Qur'an tells believers not to enter others' houses until welcomed (24:27) and forbids spying (49:12).

sources.institution: arXiv (preprint of a paper presented at ACM DIS 2016, Designing Interactive Systems)
sources.title: Norah Abokhodair and Sarah Vieweg, 'Privacy & Social Media in the Context of the Arab Gulf'
sources.quote: Depending on the context, hurma has two meanings: 1) anything that is unlawful to obtain or look at without permission or 2) a woman, a sacred space (mosque or home) or a sacred time (holy month).

sources.institution: arXiv (preprint of a paper presented at ACM DIS 2016, Designing Interactive Systems)
sources.title: Norah Abokhodair and Sarah Vieweg, 'Privacy & Social Media in the Context of the Arab Gulf'
sources.quote: We suggest that privacy as practiced in traditional Islamic cultures, especially in the Gulf, involves three aspects; awrah, hurma, and haq al-khososyah.

sources.institution: Quran.com API (Saheeh International translation)
sources.title: Qur'an 24:27 (Surat an-Nur)
sources.quote: O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your own houses until you ascertain welcome and greet [...] their inhabitants.
sources.note: [...] marks only the translator's footnote marker in the API text; no words are omitted.

sources.institution: Quran.com API (Saheeh International translation)
sources.title: Qur'an 49:12 (Surat al-Hujurat)

sources.note: Arabic: وَلَا تَجَسَّسُوا۟ (wa-lā tajassasū, "do not spy"), from api.quran.com/api/v4/quran/verses/uthmani?verse_key=49:12.

facts.statement: Alan Westin's Privacy and Freedom (1967), written for a New York City Bar committee on science and law, defined privacy as 'the claim of individuals, groups, or institutions to determine for themselves when, how, and to what extent information about them is communicated to others', and argued that it preserves autonomy, release from role-playing, self-evaluation and protected communication.

sources.institution: California Law Review (vol. 90), via GW Law Scholarly Commons (archived copy)
sources.title: Daniel J. Solove, 'Conceptualizing Privacy'
sources.quote: claim of individuals, groups, or institutions to determine for themselves when, how, and to what extent information about them is communicated to others.
sources.note: Solove p. 1109-10 quotes Westin, Privacy and Freedom (Atheneum, 1967), p. 7: "Privacy is the claim of individuals..."; the opening words sit before a page break in the PDF, so only the contiguous part is quoted. Read from the Internet Archive copy of the GW Law repository PDF (the live repository returns 403 to scripts). Canonical: https://scholarship.law.gwu.edu/faculty_publications/933/

sources.quote: Privacy, he contends, provides individuals and groups in society with a preservation of autonomy, a release from role-playing, a time for self-evaluation and for protected communication.
sources.note: Unsigned book note, 25 Wash. & Lee L. Rev. 166 (1968), read from the Internet Archive copy (the live repository returns 403 to scripts).

facts.statement: Westin argued, drawing on studies of animal territoriality, that the human need for privacy is probably rooted in our animal origins and that people and animals share basic privacy-claiming mechanisms.

sources.institution: Frontiers in Veterinary Science (vol. 8)
sources.title: Clara Mancini et al., 'The Case for Animal Privacy in the Design of Technologically Supported Environments'
sources.quote: In his seminal work on Privacy and Freedom, Westin ( 1 ) made direct reference to Ardrey ( 11 )'s writings on territoriality to argue that humans' need for privacy is likely rooted in our animal origins, and that humans and animals share a number of basic privacy-claiming mechanisms.
sources.note: Secondary (peer-reviewed) summary of Westin 1967, ch. 1 (p. 26 cited). Westin's book was not read directly.

facts.statement: Psychologist Irwin Altman concluded in 1977, from ethnographic data on many cultures, that privacy is a universal process regulated by culturally specific means - from secret forest paths among some Brazilian peoples and soft speech in Java to the Tuareg face veil - and he treated it as dynamic boundary regulation, opening as well as closing.

sources.institution: Journal of Social Issues (vol. 33, no. 3), abstract via Crossref
sources.title: Irwin Altman, 'Privacy Regulation: Culturally Universal or Culturally Specific?'
sources.quote: Ethnographic data are examined from a variety of cultures, particularly from societies with apparently maximum and minimum privacy
sources.note: Publisher abstract as deposited with Crossref; the Wiley page blocks scripts.

sources.institution: Journal of Social Issues (vol. 33, no. 3), abstract via Crossref
sources.title: Irwin Altman, 'Privacy Regulation: Culturally Universal or Culturally Specific?'
sources.quote: It is concluded that privacy is a universal process that involves culturally unique regulatory mechanisms.

sources.institution: Journal of Consumer Psychology (vol. 30, no. 4), author copy hosted by Carnegie Mellon University
sources.title: Alessandro Acquisti, Laura Brandimarte and George Loewenstein, 'Secrets and Likes: The Drive for Privacy and the Difficulty of Achieving It in the Digital Age'
sources.quote: the evidence of "privacy"-seeking behaviors across cultures and historical periods is ample (Moore, 1984; Murphy, 1964), from the use of secret paths in the woods by some tribes in Brazil, to Javanese people hiding their emotions and speaking softly, and from the rearranging of the huts by the Pygmies of Zaire in response to the arrival of new people to the camp, to the covering of almost their entire face by the Tuareg of Northern Africa (Altman, 1977).
sources.note: The examples are Altman's (1977); the source uses the dated ethnonym "Pygmies" (the Mbuti of the Ituri forest).

sources.institution: Journal of Consumer Psychology (vol. 30, no. 4), author copy hosted by Carnegie Mellon University

facts.statement: Sociologist Barrington Moore Jr., in Privacy: Studies in Social and Cultural History (1984), called the need for privacy 'a socially created need', arguing that without society there would be no need for privacy.

facts.statement: Philosopher Judith Jarvis Thomson (Philosophy & Public Affairs, 1975) observed that nobody seemed to have a clear idea what the right to privacy is, and argued that it is really a cluster of other rights - over property and over one's own person.

sources.institution: California Law Review (vol. 90), via GW Law Scholarly Commons (archived copy)
sources.title: Daniel J. Solove, 'Conceptualizing Privacy'
sources.quote: ("Perhaps the most striking thing about the right to privacy is that nobody seems to have any very clear idea what it is.")
sources.note: Solove n. 6 quotes Thomson from the reprint in Schoeman (ed.), Philosophical Dimensions of Privacy (1984), p. 272. Read from the Internet Archive copy of the GW Law repository PDF (the live repository returns 403 to scripts). Canonical: https://scholarship.law.gwu.edu/faculty_publications/933/

facts.statement: Legal philosopher Ruth Gavison (Yale Law Journal, 1980) defined privacy as limited access to a person, made up of three irreducible elements: secrecy, anonymity and solitude.

sources.quote: Further, Gavison explains what constitutes limited access, which consists of "three independent and irreducible elements: secrecy, anonymity, and solitude."

facts.statement: Daniel Solove argued in 2002 that privacy had become a 'sweeping concept' - from freedom of thought to freedom from surveillance - with no single common core, and proposed understanding it through Wittgenstein's 'family resemblances'; the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy likewise finds no single definition.

sources.institution: California Law Review (vol. 90), via GW Law Scholarly Commons (archived copy)
sources.title: Daniel J. Solove, 'Conceptualizing Privacy'
sources.quote: Currently, privacy is a sweeping concept, encompassing (among other things) freedom of thought, control over one's body, solitude in one's home, control over information about oneself, freedom from surveillance, protection of one's reputation, and protection from searches and interrogations.
sources.note: Read from the Internet Archive copy of the GW Law repository PDF (the live repository returns 403 to scripts). Canonical: https://scholarship.law.gwu.edu/faculty_publications/933/

sources.note: Read from the Internet Archive copy of the GW Law repository PDF (the live repository returns 403 to scripts). Canonical: https://scholarship.law.gwu.edu/faculty_publications/933/

facts.statement: Helen Nissenbaum's theory of contextual integrity (2004) holds that privacy is violated when information flows break the norms of the context in which it was shared - norms of appropriateness and norms of distribution.

sources.institution: Washington Law Review (vol. 79, no. 1), copy on the author's Cornell Tech site
sources.title: Helen Nissenbaum, 'Privacy as Contextual Integrity'
sources.quote: The central thesis of this Article is that the benchmark of privacy is contextual integrity; that in any given situation, a complaint that privacy has been violated is sound in the event that one or the other types of the informational norms has been transgressed.

sources.institution: Washington Law Review (vol. 79, no. 1), copy on the author's Cornell Tech site
sources.title: Helen Nissenbaum, 'Privacy as Contextual Integrity'
sources.quote: I posit two types of informational norms: norms of appropriateness, and norms of flow or distribution.

facts.statement: Julie Cohen (Harvard Law Review, 2013) argued that privacy matters less as protection for a finished 'liberal self' than as breathing room in which a self develops, shielding 'dynamic, emergent subjectivity' from commercial and government efforts to make people fixed, transparent and predictable.

sources.institution: Harvard Law Review (vol. 126, no. 7)
sources.title: Julie E. Cohen, 'What Privacy Is For'
sources.quote: Privacy shelters dynamic, emergent subjectivity from the efforts of commercial and government actors to render individuals and communities fixed, transparent, and predictable.

facts.statement: The Hippocratic Oath, perhaps the best-known Greek medical text, binds the physician to keep secret whatever he sees or hears in patients' lives that ought not to be spoken of - an early professional duty of confidentiality.

sources.institution: U.S. National Library of Medicine, History of Medicine Division

sources.quote: Whatever I see or hear in the lives of my patients, whether in connection with my professional practice or not, which ought not to be spoken of outside, I will keep secret, as considering all such things to be private.
sources.note: The page says its display was curated by Michael North, then Head of Rare Books at NLM; the translator is not otherwise named. The Oath is conventionally dated to the late 5th or 4th century BCE; the page does not date it.

sources.institution: U.S. National Library of Medicine, History of Medicine Division
sources.title: Greek Medicine: The Oath
sources.quote: The Hippocratic Oath (Ορκος) is perhaps the most widely known of Greek medical texts.

facts.statement: The Mishnah, the early rabbinic law code, forbids a person to open a window or doorway facing a courtyard shared with neighbours - a rule a modern English translation glosses as ensuring residents 'a measure of privacy'.

sources.quote: A person may not open his windows

sources.institution: Sefaria (William Davidson Edition - English, Steinsaltz)

sources.quote: so as to ensure that the residents will enjoy a measure of privacy
sources.note: This clause is the translator's explanatory interpolation (unbolded in the Davidson edition), not the Mishnah's own words. The phrase "damage by seeing" (hezek re'iyah) is from the Talmud (Bava Batra 2b-3a) and is not quoted from this page.

facts.statement: For most people the pre-modern home offered little seclusion: until the seventeenth century many homes were one large multipurpose space and beds were shared, even with guests; from the seventeenth century houses were partitioned into rooms with distinct purposes, though without corridors people still walked through each other's rooms.

facts.statement: After the Council of Trent, Archbishop Charles Borromeo of Milan published the Instructiones Fabricae et Supellectilis Ecclesiasticae (1577), whose rules for the confessional aimed to give the penitent privacy while preventing misconduct by the confessor.

sources.title: Matthew E. Gallegos, 'Charles Borromeo and Catholic Tradition Regarding the Design of Catholic Churches'
sources.quote: Borromeo published the document in 1577, and it was reprinted without major revisions at least nineteen times between 1577 and 1952.

facts.note: Popular accounts credit Borromeo with "inventing" the confessional box; this source supports only that his 1577 directives regulated confessionals for privacy and propriety.

facts.statement: In Ex parte Jackson (96 U.S. 727, October Term 1877) the U.S. Supreme Court held that sealed letters in the mail are as protected from inspection 'as if they were retained by the parties forwarding them in their own domiciles' - carrying the protection of the home to the sealed page.

sources.quote: Letters and sealed packages of this kind in the mail are as fully guarded from examination and inspection, except as to their outward form and weight, as if they were retained by the parties forwarding them in their own domiciles.
sources.note: Reported as October Term 1877 and usually cited as decided in 1878 (the LII page shows "October Term, 1877"); Solove (2002) dates it 1877.

facts.statement: In colonial America seals were weak and postal clerks were suspected of reading mail; Benjamin Franklin, in charge of the colonial post, made employees swear not to open letters, and later laws protected the mail - from which Solove concludes that privacy is 'not just found but constructed'.

facts.statement: On 15 December 1890 Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis argued in the Harvard Law Review that 'instantaneous photographs and newspaper enterprise' had invaded 'the sacred precincts of private and domestic life' and that the common law should protect what Judge Thomas Cooley had called the right 'to be let alone'.

sources.institution: University of Louisville, Louis D. Brandeis School of Law Library (Brandeis Collection)
sources.title: Samuel D. Warren and Louis D. Brandeis, 'The Right to Privacy', 4 Harvard Law Review 193
sources.quote: Instantaneous photographs and newspaper enterprise have invaded the sacred precincts of private and domestic life; and numerous mechanical devices threaten to make good the prediction that "what is whispered in the closet shall be proclaimed from the house-tops."
sources.note: Harvard Law Review vol. 4, no. 5, pp. 193-220; the issue date 15 December 1890 is from Crossref metadata for DOI 10.2307/1321160 (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/1321160, published-print 1890-12-15). The Louisville page gives "4 Harvard Law Review 193 (1890)".

sources.institution: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Beate Roessler and Judith DeCew)
sources.title: Privacy (substantive revision 19 October 2023)
sources.quote: Focusing in large part on increasing levels of publicity enabled by the burgeoning newspaper industry and recent inventions such as photography, they emphasized the invasion of privacy brought about by the public dissemination of details relating to a person's private life.

sources.institution: University of Louisville, Louis D. Brandeis School of Law Library (Brandeis Collection)
sources.title: Samuel D. Warren and Louis D. Brandeis, 'The Right to Privacy', 4 Harvard Law Review 193
sources.quote: Recent inventions and business methods call attention to the next step which must be taken for the protection of the person, and for securing to the individual what Judge Cooley calls the right "to be let alone."
sources.note: Footnote 10 of the article: "Cooley on Torts, 2d ed., p. 29." (1888).

facts.statement: Dissenting in Olmstead v. United States (4 June 1928), a wiretapping case, Justice Brandeis called the right to be let alone 'the most comprehensive of rights and the right most valued by civilized men'.

sources.institution: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (U.S. Supreme Court opinion)
sources.title: Olmstead v. United States, 277 U.S. 438 (1928), Brandeis J. dissenting
sources.quote: They conferred, as against the government, the right to be let alone-the most comprehensive of rights and the right most valued by civilized men.
sources.note: The LII text renders the dash as a hyphen ("alone-the"). Decided June 4, 1928.

facts.statement: The U.S. Constitution contains no express right to privacy; in Griswold v. Connecticut (7 June 1965) the Supreme Court found 'zones of privacy' in the penumbras of the Bill of Rights, while Justice Black, dissenting, called privacy 'a broad, abstract and ambiguous concept'.

sources.institution: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (U.S. Supreme Court opinion)
sources.title: Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U.S. 479 (1965)
sources.quote: The foregoing cases suggest that specific guarantees in the Bill of Rights have penumbras, formed by emanations from those guarantees that help give them life and substance.

sources.institution: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (U.S. Supreme Court opinion)
sources.title: Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U.S. 479 (1965)
sources.quote: Various guarantees create zones of privacy.

sources.institution: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (U.S. Supreme Court opinion)
sources.title: Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U.S. 479 (1965), Black J. dissenting
sources.quote: 'Privacy' is a broad, abstract and ambiguous concept which can easily be shrunken in meaning but which can also, on the other hand, easily be interpreted as a constitutional ban against many things other than searches and seizures.

sources.institution: Supreme Court of India, via Indian Kanoon
sources.title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (survey of US Supreme Court decisions)
sources.quote: The US Constitution does not contain an express right to privacy.

facts.statement: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948, made privacy an international human right: 'No one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with his privacy, family, home or correspondence'.

sources.institution: United Nations
sources.title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 12
sources.quote: No one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with his privacy, family, home or correspondence, nor to attacks upon his honour and reputation.

sources.institution: United Nations
sources.title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights (introduction)
sources.quote: the Declaration was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 ( General Assembly resolution 217 A ) as a common standard of achievements for all peoples and all nations.

facts.statement: Treaties followed the Declaration: the European Convention on Human Rights (signed in Rome, 4 November 1950) protects 'private and family life', home and correspondence in Article 8, and the UN's International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (adopted 16 December 1966) does so in Article 17.

sources.institution: UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (archived copy)
sources.title: International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, Article 17
sources.quote: 1. No one shall be subjected to arbitrary or unlawful interference with his privacy, family, home or correspondence, nor to unlawful attacks on his honour and reputation.
sources.note: OHCHR returns 403 to scripts; read from the Internet Archive copy. The page header gives "ADOPTED 16 December 1966 BY General Assembly resolution 2200A (XXI)". The Covenant entered into force in 1976.

sources.institution: Council of Europe / European Court of Human Rights
sources.title: Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, Article 8
sources.quote: Everyone has the right to respect for his private and family life, his home and his correspondence.

facts.statement: In 1988 the UN Human Rights Committee's General Comment 16 read Article 17 as covering data: holding personal information on computers and data banks must be regulated by law, and every individual should be able to learn, in intelligible form, whether data about them is stored and for what purposes.

sources.institution: University of Minnesota Human Rights Library (text of UN document HRI/GEN/1/Rev.1)
sources.title: Human Rights Committee, General Comment No. 16: Article 17 (Right to Privacy)
sources.quote: The gathering and holding of personal information on computers, databanks and other devices, whether by public authorities or private individuals or bodies, must be regulated by law.
sources.note: Adopted 8 April 1988 at the Committee's thirty-second session (the UMN header says "Twenty-third session, 1988", an apparent error). The UN treaty-body database offers only a .doc file.

sources.institution: University of Minnesota Human Rights Library (text of UN document HRI/GEN/1/Rev.1)
sources.title: Human Rights Committee, General Comment No. 16: Article 17 (Right to Privacy)
sources.quote: In order to have the most effective protection of his private life, every individual should have the right to ascertain in an intelligible form, whether, and if so, what personal data is stored in automatic data files, and for what purposes.

facts.statement: Of the 188 national constitutions in force in the Comparative Constitutions Project's Constitute database, 171 (about nine in ten) are coded as providing a right to privacy; the exceptions include countries such as India, France and Japan where courts rather than the text protect it.

sources.institution: Constitute Project (Comparative Constitutions Project, University of Texas at Austin / University of Chicago)
sources.title: Topics: Right to privacy
sources.quote: Grants individuals protection against government intrusion into their property, papers, person, or communications without proper authorization. Also protects against such intrusions by private individuals.
sources.note: Topic definition. Counts computed on 2026-09-23 from the Constitute API: 171 in-force constitutions returned by https://www.constituteproject.org/service/constopicsearch?key=privacy&in_force=true&lang=en out of 188 in force (https://www.constituteproject.org/service/constitutions?in_force=true&lang=en). In-force constitutions not coded for privacy: Afghanistan, Antigua and Barbuda, Australia, Austria, Bahamas, Brunei, Canada, Czech Republic, France, India, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Palau, Samoa, Singapore, Sri Lanka. Coding is of constitutional text only.

facts.note: The count is our computation from the Constitute API, not a figure the project publishes; it depends on Constitute's coding and on which constitutions it holds. The claim that courts protect privacy in India, France and Japan rests on the Puttaswamy, Article 9 and 1964 facts elsewhere in this file.

facts.statement: On 24 August 2017 all nine judges of a Supreme Court of India bench signed the order in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India overruling earlier cases and holding that privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21.

sources.title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India, Order of the Court, 24 August 2017
sources.quote: (iii) The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.
sources.note: The Order of the Court is signed by all nine judges; it also overrules M P Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) to the extent they held privacy unprotected.

sources.title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India, Order of the Court, 24 August 2017

facts.statement: In 2015 Shoshana Zuboff named 'surveillance capitalism': a logic of accumulation, read through Google's practices, whose mechanisms of extraction and control 'exile persons from their own behavior' while creating markets in behavioural prediction.

sources.title: Shoshana Zuboff, 'Big other: surveillance capitalism and the prospects of an information civilization'
sources.quote: It is constituted by unexpected and often illegible mechanisms of extraction, commodification, and control that effectively exile persons from their own behavior while producing new markets of behavioral prediction and modification.
sources.note: Abstract, as shown on the Springer landing page (published 9 April 2015). The abstract also says Google's practices are "the primary lens for this analysis".

sources.quote: The institutionalizing practices and operational assumptions of Google Inc. are the primary lens for this analysis as they are rendered in two recent articles authored by Google Chief Economist Hal Varian.

facts.statement: On 9 March 1993 Eric Hughes's 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto' distinguished privacy from secrecy - 'the power to selectively reveal oneself to the world' - and argued that people must defend it themselves, with code and cryptography.

sources.institution: activism.net (Cypherpunks archive)
sources.title: Eric Hughes, 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto'
sources.quote: Privacy is necessary for an open society in the electronic age. Privacy is not secrecy. A private matter is something one doesn't want the whole world to know, but a secret matter is something one doesn't want anybody to know. Privacy is the power to selectively reveal oneself to the world.

sources.institution: activism.net (Cypherpunks archive)
sources.title: Eric Hughes, 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto'
sources.quote: We must defend our own privacy if we expect to have any.

facts.statement: Solove (2013) named the dominant model 'privacy self-management' - notice, access and consent, largely unchanged since the 1970s - and argued it 'does not provide people with meaningful control', because consent legitimises nearly any use of data and there are too many data collectors to manage one by one.

sources.title: Daniel J. Solove, 'Introduction: Privacy Self-Management and the Consent Dilemma'
sources.quote: Policymakers have proposed and passed significant new regulation in the United States and abroad, yet the basic approach to protecting privacy has remained largely unchanged since the 1970s.

sources.institution: Harvard Law Review (vol. 126, no. 7)
sources.title: Daniel J. Solove, 'Introduction: Privacy Self-Management and the Consent Dilemma'
sources.quote: Privacy self-management does not provide people with meaningful control over their data.

sources.institution: Harvard Law Review (vol. 126, no. 7)
sources.title: Daniel J. Solove, 'Introduction: Privacy Self-Management and the Consent Dilemma'
sources.quote: Consent legitimizes nearly any form of collection, use, or disclosure of personal data.

sources.institution: Harvard Law Review (vol. 126, no. 7)
sources.title: Daniel J. Solove, 'Introduction: Privacy Self-Management and the Consent Dilemma'
sources.quote: There are too many entities collecting and using personal data to make it feasible for people to manage their privacy separately with each entity.

facts.statement: Nissenbaum (2011) called notice-and-consent's core flaw its assumption that individuals can grasp every relevant fact at the moment of 'pair-wise contracting' with a data gatherer, and named the 'transparency paradox': detailed notices go unread, simple ones leave out what matters.

sources.title: Helen Nissenbaum, 'A Contextual Approach to Privacy Online'
sources.quote: I view this as a futile effort because of what I call the transparency paradox.

sources.institution: Daedalus (vol. 140, no. 4), American Academy of Arts & Sciences - copy on the author's Cornell Tech site
sources.title: Helen Nissenbaum, 'A Contextual Approach to Privacy Online'
sources.quote: Proposals to improve and fortify notice-and-consent, such as clearer privacy policies and fairer information practices, will not overcome a fundamental flaw in the model, namely, its assumption that individuals can understand all facts relevant to true choice at the moment of pair-wise contracting between individuals and data gatherers.

facts.statement: Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University estimated in 2008 that reading the privacy policies of the sites an American visits would take about 201 hours a year, worth about $3,534 per internet user and about $781 billion nationally.

sources.quote: We estimate that reading privacy policies carries costs in time of approximately 201 hours a year, worth about $3,534 annually per American Internet user.

sources.institution: I/S: A Journal of Law and Policy for the Information Society (2008 Privacy Year in Review) - authors' pre-press version
sources.title: Aleecia M. McDonald and Lorrie Faith Cranor, 'The Cost of Reading Privacy Policies'
sources.quote: Nationally, if Americans were to read online privacy policies word-for-word, we estimate the value of time lost as about $781 billion annually.

facts.note: Both authors were at Carnegie Mellon University (author note on the first page of the pre-press PDF). The estimate assumes each policy is read once a year.

facts.statement: Doc Searls, founder of ProjectVRM and co-founder of Customer Commons, wrote in 2019 that privacy online cannot be 'a grace of privacy policies' written by each company, and that individuals should proffer terms 'as first parties' which sites agree to, with both keeping records.

sources.institution: Linux Journal
sources.title: Doc Searls, 'If Your Privacy Is in the Hands of Others Alone, You Don't Have Any'
sources.quote: And we need to be clear that privacy is not a grace of privacy policies and terms of service that differ with every company and over which none of us have true control

sources.institution: Linux Journal
sources.title: Doc Searls, 'If Your Privacy Is in the Hands of Others Alone, You Don't Have Any'
sources.quote: Sites and services can agree to those terms, and both can keep records and follow audit trails.

His bio on the page: he "continues to run ProjectVRM, which he launched at the BKC in 2006, and is a co-founder and board member of its nonprofit spinoff, Customer Commons."

facts.statement: IEEE 7012-2025, the Standard for Machine Readable Personal Privacy Terms, was approved by the IEEE Standards Board on 4 November 2025 and published on 20 January 2026; it describes how individuals, 'acting as first parties', proffer privacy terms that the other side accepts and both sides record.

myths.claim: Privacy is a modern Western invention that other cultures lack.
myths.correction: Privacy norms appear in ancient and non-Western sources - the Hippocratic Oath, the Mishnah's rule on windows, the Qur'an's command to seek permission before entering a house - and anthropologists such as Irwin Altman found privacy regulation in every culture they examined, though by culturally specific means. What is modern is the legal 'right to privacy' (from 1890) and the idea of privacy as control over data.

myths.claim: Chinese and Japanese have no word for privacy.
myths.correction: Chinese has yinsi (隐私), long carrying a connotation of shameful secrets but now defined in Article 1032 of China's 2020 Civil Code; Japanese adopted the loanword puraibashii, which spread after a 1964 Tokyo court judgment.
